name: The Alarm Clock
blurb: At six a.m. someone argues with their alarm clock and ends up reviewing their whole life
title: The Alarm Clock: Comedic Monologue Script (3 Min)
description: A 3-minute comedic monologue for 1 actor of any gender: a dawn argument with an alarm clock escalates into a full life review. Free to perform and film.
h1: The Alarm Clock: a 3-Minute Comedic Monologue for 1 Actor
logline: It is six in the morning and Sam's alarm will not stop. What starts as a negotiation over five more minutes turns into a trial, with the alarm clock as the prosecution and Sam's whole life as the evidence.
setting: A bed or a sofa with a blanket, dawn. Props: an alarm clock or a phone, a blanket, a pillow.

roles.name: Sam
roles.note: 25 to 45, any gender. Not a morning person. Wants five more minutes, and maybe a different life.

script.action: Darkness. SAM is a lump under a blanket.
A hand comes out of the blanket, hits the clock. Silence. The hand retreats.

script.say: That was not nine minutes. That was nine seconds. I know what nine minutes feels like. I've trained for this.
Okay. Okay. Let's talk like adults. One of us is an adult. I'll give you that you're very punctual. And in return you give me five minutes. Just five. Nobody has to know.
Is that a no? It sounded like a no.
Don't take that tone with me. I bought you. I chose you over a cheaper clock that played birdsong. You were on sale. Remember that.

script.action: Sam puts the clock under the pillow. Lies on the pillow.

script.sfx: Muffled beeping from under the pillow.

script.say: Fine. Fine! Why? Why do you want me up so badly? So I can catch the bus? The bus doesn't love me. The bus has never once waited for me.
Work. Yes. Thank you. I know. Do you know what I do at work? I move numbers from one screen to a different screen. And then someone moves them back. That's the job. I'm a very expensive tide.
script.how: to the clock, as if it asked

script.say: It was supposed to be temporary! I was twenty-three. It was one summer. That was eleven summers ago. You were there. You've woken me up for all of them.

script.action: Sam paces, holding the clock like a microphone.

script.say: When I was seven I wanted to be an astronaut. At twelve, a vet. At sixteen I was going to start a band. I had a name. We had a logo. We didn't have instruments, but we had a logo.
Don't laugh. That was a laughing beep, I heard it.
And what am I now? I'm a person who argues with a clock. At dawn. And loses.
script.how: sitting on the edge of the bed, suddenly deflated

script.say: What? You think I could still do it? Not astronaut, obviously. I get sick on swings. But the other stuff. Something with animals. Something I'd actually get up for.

You're right. You're right! Why am I waiting for permission? Today. I'm going in today and I'm telling them. I'm handing in my notice. I'm signing up for the evening course. I'm going to wake up for something!

script.action: Sam throws off the blanket, triumphant, and grabs a phone to check the time.

script.say: Six fifteen. Plenty of time. Saturday the... Saturday.

script.action: A long pause. Sam looks at the phone. Looks at the clock.

script.say: It's Saturday. You woke me up on a Saturday. I gave you a speech. I gave you my band.

script.action: Sam lifts the clock as if to throw it. Stops. Looks at it for a moment. Sets it down gently on the pillow.

script.say: No. You know what? Saturday is a good day to start.

script.action: Sam pulls on a jumper and heads for the door. Stops. Comes back. Turns the clock face down.

ul: A bed, a mattress or two chairs pushed together with a blanket. Set it centre and slightly angled so the audience can see Sam's face from under the blanket.
The alarm sound can be a real phone alarm triggered by a friend offstage, a recorded track, or a classmate making the beep live. A live beep player gets extra laughs because the timing can react.
Map the escalation in space: lying down, sitting up, out of bed, pacing, standing on the bed for the big speech. Then drop back to sitting for the Saturday reveal.
Use the clock as a scene partner. Hold it at eye level when you talk to it and give it real pauses to reply.
For a self-tape, frame from the foot of the bed in a wide shot and add the beeps in editing. For audio, the blanket rustle, the footsteps and the birdsong at the end carry the picture.
Treat every beep as a line of dialogue. Listen, react, then answer; the audience should feel the clock has a personality.
Start small and grumpy and build in clear steps: negotiation, accusation, life story, inspiration. Each step is a little louder than the last.
The deflated moment, a person who argues with a clock and loses, is the heart of the piece. Play it honestly for a second before the comedy returns.
Take your time on the Saturday reveal. Slow down mid-word and let the realisation land before the next line.
Do not rush the final five more minutes. It is the button on the whole piece; say it as a happy, guilty decision.
Swap the alarm for a smart speaker that answers in a calm voice, played by a second actor offstage.
Change the dreams to fit the performer: a dancer, a chef, a teacher, a footballer. The list should be personal and specific.
End differently: Sam really does go out, and the last image is Sam's alarm beeping on the pillow in an empty room.

prompts.keyframe: Dim bedroom at dawn, blue light through curtains, a person buried under a rumpled blanket with one hand reaching out towards a glowing alarm clock on the bedside table, cinematic still, 16:9, comic mood.
shots: Wide shot from the foot of the bed, static camera, a person sits up angrily and argues with an alarm clock held at eye level, early blue dawn light, comic mood.
Medium shot, handheld follow, the person paces the bedroom holding the alarm clock like a microphone and gestures passionately, building energy.
Close-up on the person's face lit by a phone screen, expression slowly sliding from triumph to disbelief, then a small smile, warm morning light rising.

faq.q: Can I use The Alarm Clock for a school drama class or a contest?
faq.a: Yes. It is an original monologue under CC BY 4.0, so you can perform, film and post it anywhere, including monetised channels. Credit Script: cv.cm.

faq.q: How do I do the beeps if I am performing alone?
faq.a: Record a short alarm sound and play it from a phone in your pocket or ask someone offstage to trigger it. In a self-tape, add the beeps in editing and leave a clear pause after each line for them.

faq.q: Does the joke still work in countries where people work on Saturdays?
faq.a: Yes. Change Saturday to whichever day is a rest day for you, such as Sunday or a public holiday. The twist only needs a day when no alarm was needed.
